affected.title: vCenter before the fix
affected.body: Below 9.1.1.0200, 9.0.2.0200 or 8.0 U3m. On VMware Cloud Foundation 5.x, you're affected until vCenter is on 8.0 U3m, which VCF 5.2.5 includes (for Telco Cloud, see Broadcom KB463116). vCenter 7.0 is affected too, and Mandiant says the attackers' tool works on 7.x and 8.x; Broadcom says to presume 6.5 and 6.7 are affected. The bug is in vCenter's directory service; Broadcom's FAQ says ESX isn't affected. 1,2,4,5

affected.title: An attacker can reach vCenter
affected.body: Network access to vCenter is enough; no login is needed. In the attack Mandiant investigated, the attackers first broke into another machine on the internal network, then reached vCenter's single sign-on port 2012 from there. 1,2

actions.title: Patch now
actions.body: Install 9.1.1.0200, 9.0.2.0200 or 8.0 U3m (on VCF 5.x, patch vCenter to 8.0 U3m or move to VCF 5.2.5); Broadcom's patches are cumulative, so later versions also fix it. Broadcom gives no workaround. CISA's deadline for US agencies is 23 Nov 2026. 8.0 U3m and 9.0.2.0200 blocked upgrades to VCF 9.1.1; VCF 9.1.2 (24 Nov 2026) removes that block. The same advisory also covers four lesser bugs that need an account or local access, in SDDC Manager and VMware Tools for Windows (CVE-2026-123891 to CVE-2026-123894), with their own fixed versions. Broadcom's 24 Nov advisory fixes a second login bypass in the same service ( VMware Nov fixes ): vCenter 8.0 U3m covers both, but 9.1 and 9.0 need 9.1.2 or 9.0.2.0300. 1,3,5,6,7 Latest safe versions checked 24 Nov VMware vCenter → 9.1 9.1.2 9.0 9.0.2.0300 8.0 8.0 U3m VMware Cloud Foundation 5.x: patch vCenter to 8.0 U3m, or move to VCF 5.2.5, which includes it.

actions.title: On vCenter 7.0?
actions.body: Broadcom lists no public fix for 7.0 and tells customers with an extended support contract to contact Broadcom Support to request patches. Without one, there is no fix for 7.0. 1,5

actions.title: Limit who can reach vCenter
actions.body: Mandiant recommends a default-deny firewall on vCenter that allows its management ports, including 443 and 2012, only from an allowlist of trusted hosts. In its write-up, allowlisting port 2012 would have stopped the exploit, and allowlisting 443 would have stopped the attackers using the logins they forged. This adds protection; it doesn't replace the patch. 2

actions.title: Check for a break-in
actions.body: Patching doesn't remove attackers who are already in, and CISA flags this one for forensic triage. Look for single sign-on administrator accounts you didn't create, and for Mandiant's file indicators, such as /tmp/123 , /tmp/sss , /tmp/dbr and /usr/bin/vmtoolscs , on other internal Linux machines the attackers took over. The attackers also took vCenter's SAML signing key, which lets them forge logins for any user. 2,3

affected.title: MiCollab, not patched
affected.body: Mitel lists MiCollab 10.3 (10.3.0.18) and earlier as affected. The fix is a patch for 10.3.0.18, so 10.3.0.18 without it is still affected. Mitel doesn't consider versions past End of Support. 1,4

affected.title: An attacker can reach AWV
affected.body: All five bugs are in the Audio, Web and Video Conferencing (AWV) component and need no login: a blind command injection (CVE-2026-133323, 10.0), command execution through XML injection with content planted in advance (CVE-2026-133303, 9.0), and three medium bugs that upload files, skip a login check or read some sensitive information. Mitel's workaround is to restrict external access to AWV. At Accenture's victim the attack passed through an internet-facing reverse proxy, and Accenture says a MiVoice Border Gateway web proxy shouldn't be assumed to protect AWV. 1,8

actions.title: Apply Mitel's patch
actions.body: Upgrade to 10.3.0.18 if needed, then apply Mitel's patch from knowledge base article KB000129195, which is restricted: if you can't open it, Mitel says to contact your Mitel Authorized Partner. Mitel also offers upgrading to a later release but names none. Accenture advises taking forensic images of MiCollab and Border Gateway servers before patching or rebuilding them, because that can overwrite evidence, and fixing older MiCollab flaws (MISA-2026-0006) on servers that have fallen behind. 1,8

actions.title: Cut outside access to AWV
actions.body: Mitel's workaround until you can patch: restrict external access to the AWV component. Accenture adds: include any path a MiVoice Border Gateway web proxy publishes. 1,8

actions.title: Check for a break-in
actions.body: Accenture says a server that is patched now may already be compromised, because attacks began before the patch existed. Compare MiCollab's logs with your proxy, gateway or WAF logs, since the attacker filtered its requests out of local logs. Look for web shells such as shell.asp under a pictures directory, scripts and .tgz archives in /tmp , round-the-clock HTTPS to unfamiliar hosts, and traffic to 204.76.203.204 or 204.76.203.216 ; Accenture lists more indicators. If you find signs, Accenture says to treat it as an Active Directory compromise: reset MiCollab's LDAP connector account and any Kerberoastable service accounts, and rotate administrator, SIP trunk and file-share credentials the server could reach. Federal Civilian Executive Branch (FCEB) agencies must also do CISA's forensic triage for CVE-2026-133323 and CVE-2026-133303. 8,2,3

actions.title: Why it's Patch now
actions.body: CISA lists all five as exploited and they need no login. Accenture saw them used before any patch existed and, at one victim, to reach the domain controller. It says MiCollab is commonly internet-facing, and a reverse proxy in front of it didn't protect AWV. 2,3,8

detail.name: Check Point Mgmt
detail.verdictHint: Two bugs exploited, no login, public exploit. In KEV.
detail.meterHint: Attackers are already on it. Patch now.

affected.title: Management server without the latest fix
affected.body: Security Management Server or Multi-Domain Security Management (MDS) on R82.20 without its Security Hotfix or Jumbo Hotfix Take 10, or below R82.10 Take 45, R82 Take 127 or R81.20 Take 170 (the CVE-2026-93616 record lists only R82.20 with no Jumbo Hotfix as affected); Log Server, Multi-Domain Log Server and SmartEvent have CVE-2026-93616 too; CVE-2026-16232's advisory doesn't list R82.20. R81.10 Take 192 fixes only CVE-2026-93616. No fix is listed for R81, R80.40, R80.30, R80.20, R80.10, R80 or R77.30: CVE-2026-16232 affects R77.30, R80, R80.10, R80.20, R80.30, R81 and R81.10, and CVE-2026-93616 affects R80 to R81.10, R80.40 included. Check Point says Smart-1 Cloud is already protected from both. 1,11,3,13,7,2

affected.title: Attacker can reach it over the network
affected.body: No login is needed for either bug. CVE-2026-93616 is in the management web service, and Check Point's fix-in-the-meantime is to allow TCP 19009 only from trusted IPs. CVE-2026-16232 needs internet access to the server's IP and Trusted Clients (GUI clients) that aren't restricted to trusted addresses; Rapid7 found that was the default in its testing. The Metasploit module for it uses TCP 18190 and 19009. 11,12,1,8,9

actions.title: Why it's Patch now
actions.body: Both bugs are exploited, need no login and sit on the same server. For CVE-2026-93616, Check Point names no setting that blocks it, only limiting who can reach the server, and TCP 19009 is the management web service SmartConsole connects to for login, so we'd expect it on every management server. For CVE-2026-16232, the Trusted Clients setting it needs was the default in Rapid7's tests. So we treat any unpatched management server an attacker can reach as exposed. 11,12,1,8

actions.title: Install the latest Jumbo Hotfix
actions.body: Rapid7 says customers "should install the latest Jumbo Hotfix on an emergency basis". The first takes that fix both bugs are R82.20 Take 10 (or the R82.20 Security Hotfix, no reboot), R82.10 Take 45, R82 Take 127 and R81.20 Take 170; Check Point says LivePatch Take 28/29 doesn't fix CVE-2026-93616. On R81.10, Take 192 fixes CVE-2026-93616 but Check Point lists no fix for CVE-2026-16232, and older versions get neither, so the only full fix is moving to a supported version. 7,11,1,12 Latest safe versions checked 25 Nov Check Point Security Management → R82.20 R82.20 Take 10 R82.10 R82.10 Take 45 R82 R82 Take 127 R81.20 R81.20 Take 170 Check Point says Smart-1 Cloud is already protected.

actions.title: Limit who can reach it
actions.body: In SmartConsole, under Manage & Settings > Permissions & Administrators > Trusted Clients, allow only specific trusted IPs or subnets, never the Type "Any". Allow TCP 19009 only from trusted IPs, put the management server behind a firewall, and if implied rules for control connections are on, keep Trusted Clients to trusted internal addresses. For CVE-2026-16232, Check Point also says to make sure implied rules for control connections are enabled. Rapid7 notes this lowers exposure but doesn't fix the bugs. 1,11,2,7

actions.title: Check the logs for both bugs
actions.body: CVE-2026-16232: in SmartConsole's Audit Logs (Logs & Monitor, or Logs & Events), search for Authentication method: application token and Authentication method: Password based application token ; Check Point says to treat any hit as suspicious and check for admin names or IPs you don't know, and lists attacker IPs for events before 23 Jul 2026. CVE-2026-93616: in Expert mode, search the cpm.elg* logs under $MDS_FWDIR/log for login requests with usernames over 1,000 characters (then look for FWM or MDS core dumps from the same time in /var/log/dump/usermode/ ), and for "Invoking method", "Uploading file" or "The path to the jars" entries with ../ or encoded traversal. Check Point says a match isn't proof. Rapid7 says to check even after patching if the server was reachable. 1,11,7

actions.title: Look for GT13's traces
actions.body: GreyNoise's signs: a preload entry for /usr/lib/.libproc.so in /etc/ld.so.preload (it says this may mean an implant), a certificate named pivot.p12 , and unexpected policy unloads. It also lists GT13's domain newpayapp[.]com and its subdomains, and the IPs it used, "either egresses through ExpressVPN or compromised victim Check Point devices". 5

actions.title: If you find signs
actions.body: Neither Check Point nor GreyNoise gives clean-up steps; Check Point points to its support team for help. GT13 copied firewall databases and the Internal CA and made a new certificate ( pivot.p12 ), so we would treat the firewall configuration, admin credentials and Internal CA as stolen: rotate admin credentials, remove admins and certificates you don't recognise, and make sure your security policies are installed again. 2,5

cves.line: Exploited for root on clustered systems, no login.

detail.name: Cisco Expressway
detail.verdictHint: Exploited for root on clustered systems, no login.
detail.meterHint: Attackers are already on it. Patch now.

affected.title: Expressway before X15.5.20
affected.body: Expressway-C or Expressway-E, virtual or appliance, on X15.5.3 or earlier. X14 and earlier get no fix of their own: Cisco says to migrate to a fixed release. 1

affected.title: Set up as a cluster
affected.body: Cisco lists only clustered systems as affected; cluster peers are set under System > Clustering. Sources differ on the TLS verification setting: Cisco says client certificates aren't checked when TLS Verify Mode is set to Enabled, while the public exploit was tested in Permissive mode, the default, and not in Enforce mode. Cisco doesn't name the setting as a condition, so treat every clustered system as affected. 1,4,9

affected.title: An attacker can reach it
affected.body: Network access to the cluster database is enough; no login is needed. The public exploit connects on TCP port 4372, and F6 says to restrict TCP 4371–4372. In the attack F6 investigated, attackers first broke into two internet-facing Expressways on X15.5.3, then used one of them to reach two more cluster nodes on the internal network. 1,3,4

actions.title: Upgrade now
actions.body: Go to X15.5.20 or later; X14 and earlier must migrate to a fixed release. Cisco gives no workaround. CISA gave US federal civilian agencies 3 days, until 23 Nov 2026, plus a check for a break-in. That deadline binds only those agencies, under BOD 26-04; for everyone else, the listing means it's being exploited. Before upgrading a cluster: X15.5.20 supports clusters only with TLS verification set to Enforcing, and its upgrade check stops if a peer's certificate lacks its FQDN in the SAN or peers mix IP addresses and FQDNs, so switch to Enforcing and fix certificates first. The same release fixes eight more CVEs (CVE-2026-76490 to CVE-2026-76497) for groups of bugs Cisco found itself, which it says aren't known to be exploited. 1,2,6,7,8 Latest safe versions checked 23 Nov Cisco Expressway → X15.5 X15.5.22 Earlier X15 releases upgrade to X15.5. For X14 and earlier, Cisco says to migrate to a fixed release.

actions.title: Can't upgrade yet? Limit the ports
actions.body: As a stopgap, F6 recommends a firewall rule that allows TCP 4371–4372 only from your other cluster nodes. Cisco lists no workaround, so this adds protection; it doesn't replace the upgrade. 3,1

actions.title: Check for a break-in
actions.body: Upgrading doesn't remove attackers who are already in, and CISA flags this one for forensic triage. F6's signs: the entry nodeup,'wombat@127.0.0.1' in Expressway's Erlang log ( erlang.log ), Python files matching /mnt/harddisk/i{0-9}{4}[a-zA-Z]?/*.py , and the addresses 66.179.31.32 and 18.130.47.116 . If you find the log entry, F6 says to check other logs and artifacts to confirm. In its case the attackers went on to scan the network, find open file shares, work with SQL Server and WinRM, and search GitLab repositories for credentials. CISA and F6 report exploitation; Cisco's advisory, updated on 23 Nov 2026 to note the KEV listing, says Cisco itself "does not have direct evidence of active exploitation". 1,2,3

affected.title: GeoServer, not updated
affected.body: Affected: 2.27.6 and earlier, 2.28.0 to 2.28.5, and 3.0.0 to 3.0.1; 2.27.7, 2.28.6 and 3.0.2 are fixed. 2.26 and older are affected and have no fixed release. To see your version, log in to the web admin and open the About GeoServer page: Build Information lists it. 1,2,3,4,5,19,17,15

affected.title: WFS and admin are reachable
affected.body: The attack starts with an anonymous WFS request and then acts as admin: CryptoCat lists network access to WFS and the REST API as the preconditions, and for Eye Security's last step (CVE-2026-120704) GeoServer's advice is to restrict both the web admin console and the REST API, so blocking REST alone doesn't rule you out. GeoServer's default rules limit creating stored queries to admins, which the x/WFS bug skips, and rememberme is one of the login filters GeoServer sets up by default. CryptoCat and Eye Security say their chains work on a default installation with no configuration changes; watchTowr agrees. The public exploit targets the stock admin account, which is enabled by default. The public exploit needs a Linux server; Eye Security says its route also works on Windows. 3,6,10,11,13,15,18

actions.title: Update GeoServer
actions.body: 3.0.2 (stable), 2.28.6 (maintenance) or 2.27.7. GeoServer announced all three on 19 Oct 2026, more than a month before the advisories went public on 23 Nov; the researcher dates 2.28.6 to 2 Nov. 2.27 is end-of-life: GeoServer says to apply 2.27.7 as a mitigation only and plan a move to 2.28 or 3.0. Unless GEOSERVER_REMEMBERME_KEY is set, fixed releases make a new random remember-me key each time they start, so remember-me cookies stop working after the update and after every restart. In a cluster, set it to the same long value on every node; then that key is used and restarts don't change it. If you suspect exposure, GeoServer says to change admin passwords. 1,7,8,9,11,13,18,20 Latest safe versions checked 26 Nov GeoServer → 3.0 3.0.2 2.28 2.28.6 2.27 2.27.7 GeoServer 2.26 and older are end-of-life and get no fixes: move to 3.0 or 2.28.

actions.title: If you can't update yet
actions.body: GeoServer's stopgaps: block requests whose service parameter contains / , in the query string or in the service attribute of an XML request, at a proxy in front of GeoServer; remove rememberme from the web filter chain (Security > Authentication); limit the REST API's /rest/resource and /rest/security endpoints to trusted networks; disable WFS if you don't need it; and don't install JDBC drivers you don't need, such as SQLite, which Eye Security's route relies on. Changing the remember-me key alone doesn't help, because the same file read reveals the new key. 1,2,3,4,6

actions.title: Look for signs
actions.body: Check the data directory's wfs/query and workspaces/*/wfs/query folders for stored queries you didn't create; the probes watchTowr saw create stored queries. watchTowr also suggests looking for unexpected JDBC user or role services, database files in the data directory you didn't upload and admin sessions created through remember-me cookies. The public exploit deletes its stored query, JDBC service and staging folder when it's done, and Eye Security's route uses the built-in GetFeatureById stored query and creates none, so a clean result doesn't prove nothing happened. If you find signs, change admin passwords; we would also treat the server as taken over, since the exploit runs commands as the GeoServer process, which is root in the official Docker image it was tested on. 1,2,3,10,12,13,15

detail.name: SSHole
detail.verdictHint: Exploited, in CISA KEV. Alpine-style sshd only.
detail.meterHint: Attackers are already on it. Patch now.

affected.title: sshd uses musl libc
affected.body: Alpine and other musl-based systems, including Alpine containers that run sshd. glibc systems (Debian, Ubuntu, Fedora, RHEL) and Dropbear are not affected. A line with ld-musl means musl. 2,5,7 ldd "$(command -v sshd)" | grep -i musl

affected.title: PAM off, password login on
affected.body: Alpine's openssh-server is built without PAM, so sshd -T prints no usepam line. openssh-server-pam with UsePAM yes is safe. passwordauthentication yes is the default. Run as root. 1,2,8 sshd -T | grep -Ei '^(passwordauthentication|usepam|permitrootlogin) '

affected.title: A * account plus a real hash
affected.body: Some account has * as its password (key-only users, root since about Alpine 3.16 if PermitRootLogin yes , the alpine user in cloud images 3.18.11–3.24.3) and at least one account has a $5$ or $6$ hash. Directory-service users (nslcd, winbind, sssd) with no shadow entry also count, and the commands below miss them. Locked ! accounts are safe. Run as root; the second command counts real hashes. 2 awk -F: '$2=="*"{print $1}' /etc/shadow; grep -cE '^[^:]*:\$[56]\$' /etc/shadow

affected.title: openssh below the fixed package
affected.body: Upstream: OpenSSH before 10.6p2, which works around the bug in sshd; OpenSSH says the root cause is outside sshd. Alpine's fixed packages are listed under Upgrade. 9,2,1 apk info -v | grep '^openssh'

actions.title: Upgrade openssh, then restart
actions.body: Install the fixed package for your Alpine branch (listed below; fixes go back to 3.16). Run apk upgrade -U -a , then rc-service sshd restart : upgrading alone leaves the old sshd running. Other musl builds: OpenSSH 10.6p2. musl itself hasn't changed yet: on 9 Nov 2026 its maintainer said musl 1.2.7 will probably stop returning * when crypt() fails, but it isn't decided. 1,2,3,11 Latest safe versions checked 24 Nov OpenSSH → Upstream 10.6p2 Alpine edge 10.6_p2-r0 Alpine 3.24 10.3_p1-r2 Alpine 3.23 10.2_p1-r1 Alpine 3.22 10.0_p1-r11 Alpine 3.21 9.9_p2-r1 Alpine 3.20 9.7_p1-r6 Alpine 3.19 9.6_p1-r3 Alpine 3.16 to 3.18 are fixed too: 9.0_p1-r6, 9.1_p1-r7, 9.3_p2-r4.

actions.title: Can't upgrade? Turn off passwords
actions.body: In sshd_config (or a drop-in in /etc/ssh/sshd_config.d/ on Alpine 3.19+). Also set any PasswordAuthentication yes inside Match blocks to no; a drop-in doesn't override those. Check key login works, validate with sshd -t , then restart sshd and confirm sshd -T shows passwordauthentication no . 2 PasswordAuthentication no

actions.title: Look for break-ins
actions.body: A password login for root , alpine or any key-only user is a red flag. Also review doas use, new users, new authorized_keys entries and changed files. If you can't rule out a login, treat the host as compromised. US federal agencies must also do forensic triage under the KEV listing. 2,4 grep 'Accepted password for' /var/log/messages

affected.title: An unpatched vSphere system
affected.body: vCenter below 9.1.2, 9.0.2.0300 or 8.0 U3m; ESX below 9.1.2, 9.0.2.0200 or 8.0 U3m (ESXi80U3m-25926933); ESX 8.0 U3m came out on 19 Nov 2026, so an ESX 8 host already on that build is fixed. If you installed vCenter 8.0 U3m for VMSA-2026-0009 (19 Nov 2026), vCenter is already fixed, but ESX wasn't part of that advisory. vSphere 7.0 is affected, with fixes only for extended-support customers, and Broadcom says to presume 6.5 and 6.7 are too. VMware Cloud Foundation 5.x is fixed in 5.2.5. vCenter shows its build on the vSphere Client's Summary tab; the command lists your ESX hosts' builds. 1,2,6 Get-VMHost | Select-Object Name, Version, Build

affected.title: An attacker can reach that system
affected.body: The vCenter bypass needs network access to vCenter (Broadcom doesn't say which port; the public exploit talks to its directory service on LDAP port 389, or 636 with TLS); the ESX bugs need network access to the host's I/O filter service (the IOFilterVP firewall rule, port 9080 on ESX 8). No login, no user action and no VM access are needed. On ESX 8, the command lists which addresses may reach that service; Broadcom's KB uses it to check the restriction. 1,2,3,7 esxcli network firewall ruleset allowedip list -r iofiltervp
code: esxcli network firewall ruleset allowedip list -r iofiltervp

actions.title: Patch vCenter and ESX
actions.body: vCenter: 9.1.2, 9.0.2.0300 or 8.0 U3m. ESX: 9.1.2 (ESXi-9.1.2.0-25946735), 9.0.2.0200 (ESXi-9.0.2.0200-25953133) or 8.0 U3m (ESXi80U3m-25926933), including vSAN Witness Appliances. VMware Cloud Foundation 5.x applies vCenter and ESX 8.0 U3m through Broadcom's asynchronous patching guide (KB 88287). Updating ESX 9.1 or 8.0 restarts each host, and the vCenter updates can't use Quick Patch. Broadcom's Q&A says no ESX update here can be live-patched, but the ESX 9.0.2.0200 release notes call it live-patchable with no reboot. On ESX 9.0, two moderate bugs (CVE-2026-123914 and CVE-2026-123915) are still waiting for a patch. Broadcom's advisory gives no order; we'd patch vCenter first: its bypass has public exploit code, and Broadcom lists no workaround for it; its Q&A leaves firewall limits to you. Then ESX, starting with hosts that untrusted networks or many machines can reach. After patching, we'd also check the Administrators group in vCenter's single sign-on domain for accounts you don't recognise, since the public exploit can add one there. 1,2,5,7 Latest safe versions checked 24 Nov VMware vCenter → 9.1 9.1.2 9.0 9.0.2.0300 8.0 8.0 U3m VMware Cloud Foundation 5.x: patch vCenter to 8.0 U3m, or move to VCF 5.2.5, which includes it.

actions.title: Can't patch ESX 8 yet? Limit port 9080
actions.body: Broadcom's KB 463535 says to let only vCenter's address reach the IOFilterVP service on ESX 8: esxcli network firewall ruleset set -r iofiltervp --allowed-all false , then esxcli network firewall ruleset allowedip add -r iofiltervp -i <vCenter-IP> . Its Q&A warns that limiting this service covers only part of the advisory and may affect the cluster and workload availability, so patch anyway. 3,2

actions.title: Also update Workstation, Fusion, Tools and Avi
actions.body: Workstation and Fusion 26H1u1 fix the VM escape (CVE-2026-123912). VMware Tools 13.1.10 or 12.5.6 fixes a denial of service in the VGAuth service; updating ESX doesn't update Tools inside VMs. Avi Load Balancer 32.1.4 fixes all eight Avi bugs, each of which needs an Avi login, most of them admin rights. 1,2

actions.title: Why it's Patch now
actions.body: Exploit code for the vCenter bypass has been public on GitHub since 24 Nov 2026. It needs only network access to vCenter and no password; the account it names by default, administrator@vsphere.local , is one Broadcom advises keeping. Broadcom says the bug is in vCenter itself, whether or not you use Enhanced Linked Mode, and lists no workaround. Broadcom's advisory and Q&A still mention no exploitation, and none of the 23 bugs is on CISA's exploited list (catalog of 24 Nov 2026). We found no public exploit for the ESX bugs, and no independent confirmation yet that the vCenter one works. 7,8,2,1,4

detail.name: Drupal installer
detail.verdictHint: Both bugs exploited, no login. First in CISA KEV.
detail.meterHint: Attackers are already on it. Patch now.

affected.title: Drupal core, not updated
affected.body: Affected: before 10.6.23, 11.0.0 up to 11.3.22, and 11.4.0 up to 11.4.13; 11.4.14, 11.3.23 and 10.6.23 are fixed. Sites that installed only the 18 Nov releases (11.4.13, 11.3.22 or 10.6.22) are still affected. Drupal 11.2 and below, 10.5 and below, and Drupal 8 and 9 are end-of-life and get no fix. The command prints your version. 15,1,11 drush status --field=drupal-version

affected.title: An attacker can reach install.php
affected.body: Attacks go through the installer at /core/install.php , which stays reachable after installation unless you block it. Drupal says sites that have already secured the installer aren't vulnerable to the second bug. Horizon3 notes this isn't only about internet-facing sites: internal and staging sites count if an attacker can reach them. Drupal's check: each of these URLs on your site should end with 403 or 404 ; a 200 means the installer isn't blocked. Also try /core/install.php/foo and, following redirects ( curl -IL ), /install.php . 15,1,3,4 curl -I https://example.com/core/install.php

affected.title: A setup Drupal calls uncommon
affected.body: Drupal rates both bugs as needing an uncommon setup ( TD:Uncommon ) and doesn't list which. For the second bug it says sites in "unusual or incomplete install states" stayed vulnerable after the first fix, and that you can't tell from the user interface whether yours is one. A related, older hole is public: on Drupal's issue 3455853, a site whose translation import was left pending or failed lets install.php run again and replace the admin account. Drupal release manager catch says the first fix closes it "as a by-product". A 2025 report of install.php offering to reinstall a finished site, not translation-related, was closed by catch, who said the first fix "should have resolved this issue too". The proof of concept plants a similar unfinished installer state by hand. For the first bug, Drupal says some exploit paths, but not all, are blocked if the web server can't write to or change permissions on settings.php ; the 18 Nov releases stopped the installer fixing those permissions. 15,1,12,14,13,6,8

actions.title: Block install.php first
actions.body: Drupal recommends blocking the installer in the web server, which survives core updates, and says sites that have already secured it aren't vulnerable to the second bug. nginx: add the block below to the HTTPS server block; Drupal says to use ^~ , not an exact match ( = ), which on some servers doesn't block /core/install.php/foo . Apache: in the virtual host, <Location "/core/install.php"> with Require all denied . Apache without access to the virtual host: Drupal's docs also give an .htaccess rule ( <Files "install.php"> with Require all denied ), but Composer overwrites .htaccess , so lines added by hand are lost. Test with nginx -t or apachectl configtest before reloading, then rerun the check above. Drupal Steward sites with its recommended mitigations are already protected from the known attack paths for both bugs, but should still update. 3,15,1 location ^~ /core/install.php { return 404; }

actions.title: Check for a takeover, before update.php
actions.body: Drupal's guide says to run its checks before database updates, because the update rewrites the install state they read, and to copy your web server logs somewhere safe now, since some hosts keep them only a few days. The command prints the install state: anything other than done means the site is vulnerable now, but done doesn't prove it's safe, because a successful attack also sets it. Drupal says any site that left its installer reachable after the first fix may still have been compromised, and a site that was taken over may no longer be in the vulnerable state, so a clean-looking site isn't proof. Check your logs for changes to user 1, the site's first admin account, or made by it; make sure user 1's email address is one you control, and consider resetting its password. The public proof of concept replaces user 1's name, email and password, so the old admin password stops working; content is left in place. In your web logs since 18 Nov 2026, an installed site answers every installer request with 200 , so that alone isn't a sign; Drupal says to look into POST requests to /core/install.php that return 302 or 303 , much larger responses, and many installer requests from one address within minutes. If you find signs, follow Drupal's "Your Drupal site got hacked" guide and assume the attacker had admin rights and may have run code on the server. Federal Civilian Executive Branch (FCEB) agencies must also do CISA's forensic triage. 20,15,6,1,2 drush state:get install_task

actions.title: Update Drupal
actions.body: 11.4.14, 11.3.23 or 10.6.23 (25 Nov 2026), then run update.php once you've done the checks above. Drupal says the code update closes the hole right away, and the update hook then repairs sites stuck in the vulnerable state. The 25 Nov release notes say they also fix the theme registry bug the 18 Nov releases introduced ("Theme hook field not found", seen with Search API), and that a Symfony security update from the same day isn't included, so update Symfony too. 11.3 and 10.6 get security fixes only until Drupal 11.5.0 comes out in December 2026; on 11.2, 10.5 or older, move to a supported line. 15,16,17,18,9,10,20 Latest safe versions checked 26 Nov Drupal core → 11.4 11.4.14 11.3 11.3.23 10.6 10.6.23 Drupal 11.2 and below, 10.5 and below, and Drupal 8 and 9 are end-of-life and get no security fixes: move to a supported line.

actions.title: Why it's Patch now
actions.body: Drupal rates the exploitable setups as uncommon ( TD:Uncommon ) but doesn't list them, and says the user interface doesn't show whether a site is in the vulnerable state, so you can't rule your site out. install.php stays reachable unless you block it, attacks on live sites are reported for both bugs, and the first is in CISA KEV. A related, older hole in the installer was already being probed: on 28 Oct 2025 someone on Drupal's issue 3455853 reported automated requests trying to exploit it. The workaround is one web server rule. 1,15,5,12,3,2

detail.verdictHint: Exploited, no login, runs as root. In CISA KEV.

checklist.text: ✓ On CISA's exploited list (fix by 28 Nov) 2

affected.title: You run a Session Smart Conductor
affected.body: The CVE record and the bulletin's entry for this bug name only the Conductor. Sources disagree on routers: the bulletin's header says these issues affect all versions of both Session Smart Router and Conductor, and CISA's KEV entry names both. Routers need the same update anyway: the bulletin fixes 17 other bugs, among them CVE-2026-103409 (9.8), admin rights with no login on a Session Smart Router that isn't yet onboarded to Mist or a Conductor. 3,1,2,11

affected.title: Not on a fixed release
affected.body: Affected: before 7.0.5, 7.1.0 up to 7.1.6, and 7.2 before 7.2.3. Fixed: 7.0.5, 7.1.7, 7.2.3 and every later release. The 6.x lines get no fix: 6.2 is still supported until 6 Mar 2027 but past End of Engineering, and Juniper doesn't evaluate releases past End of Engineering or End of Life. 3,1,4,12

actions.title: Update the Conductor
actions.body: 7.0.5-14-lts, 7.1.7-15-sts, 7.2.3-8r2 or any later release. All three came out between 20 Aug and 29 Sep 2026, before the bug was disclosed. On 6.2 or 6.3, move to 7.0.5 or later. Update routers to a fixed release too, for the other bugs in the same bulletin. 8,9,10,12,1 Latest safe versions checked 26 Nov Juniper Session Smart Router and Conductor → 7.2 7.2.5-9r2 7.1 7.1.8-9-sts 7.0 7.0.7-2-lts

actions.title: Limit who can reach it
actions.body: Juniper says there's no workaround, but tells customers to "take steps to mitigate" until they upgrade, without saying which. Our advice: allow only your routers to reach the Conductor. Juniper's own deployment guide already says to restrict public-facing inbound access to 4505/TCP, 4506/TCP and 930/TCP, the ports routers use; Juniper doesn't say which port the attack uses, so this narrows exposure but doesn't close the hole. 1,7,5,6

actions.title: Check for a break-in
actions.body: A successful attack runs commands as root on the system that manages your routers. Juniper's bulletin gives no signs of attack to look for. Our advice: if an unpatched Conductor was reachable from the internet, treat it as possibly compromised and check it before trusting it again. Federal Civilian Executive Branch (FCEB) agencies must do CISA's forensic triage. 3,1,2,13

actions.title: Why it's Patch now
actions.body: Juniper has a report of it being exploited and it's in CISA KEV. It needs no login and gives root. Juniper names no setting that blocks it, no workaround and no port, so you can't rule out a reachable Conductor. 1,2,3

affected.title: It renders files from outsiders

Common routes: image or PDF previews through ImageMagick/Imagick, Pillow (EPS files, once pixels are loaded) or libvips with ImageMagick loaders; these check the file's content, not its name, so a .png upload counts. affected.title: You run SGLang (any version)
affected.body: The CVE record for CVE-2026-15969 lists v0.5.15 and earlier, but no fixed version has been named. As of 24 Nov 2026 the advisories still list no patched version, and v0.5.23 (2 Nov) is the newest release. With no fixed release, treat every version as affected as a precaution. 3,6,7,8 pip show sglang

affected.title: Its HTTP port is reachable by attackers
affected.body: By default SGLang listens only on 127.0.0.1, port 30000. You're exposed if it was started with --host 0.0.0.0, published from a container or Kubernetes, or put behind a proxy that forwards every route. API keys alone don't close it: the LoRA tensor route has no auth check when LoRA is on, and /server_info can leak the keys. Admin routes are open when no keys are set. Changes merged on 7 and 14 Nov stop /server_info leaking keys and make admin routes need an admin key (the current docs already describe this), but no release includes them yet. 4,5,11,12 ss -ltnp | grep 30000

actions.title: Keep SGLang off untrusted networks
actions.body: Bind it to 127.0.0.1 or a private network, segment inference hosts, and firewall the port. If clients must reach it, put a reverse proxy in front that allows only the inference routes you use and blocks everything else, including /server_info. 2,4,8

actions.title: Set separate user and admin API keys
actions.body: Start with both --api-key and --admin-api-key, and block /server_info, which gives the admin key to anyone holding the user key. This doesn't fix the LoRA tensor bug, so it's no substitute for network limits. 4,5

actions.title: Turn off pickle IPC and unused features
actions.body: Set SGLANG_USE_PICKLE_IPC to false (it defaults to true). Don't enable LoRA, the dumper (DUMPER_SERVER_PORT), remote weight updates or distributed weight routes unless you need them. Prefer safetensors and refuse untrusted .bin/.pt checkpoints. 2,4

actions.title: Was it exposed? Rotate keys, check logs
actions.body: /server_info returns the API keys and SSL key password, so rotate them. Make sure API keys and prompts aren't written to logs; NEAR AI lost two customers' API keys that way. Watch for an upstream fix and update when one ships. 1,4,8

affected.title: Kernel 4.4 or later, unpatched
affected.body: The bug came in with a 2015 change in kernel 4.4. Upstream fixed it in 5.10.275, 5.15.226, 6.1.193, 6.6.163, 6.12.117, 6.18.63, 7.3.4 and 7.4-rc2. Red Hat says RHEL 6 and 7 are not affected. Distro kernels backport, so compare with your distro's version under Update. 2,3,4 uname -r

affected.title: A TCP port the attacker can reach
affected.body: Any service that listens on TCP, such as Nginx, Apache or SSH in their default setup, with no login needed. The attack uses SYN cookies, which Kim says are on by default on most distributions. If the service runs in a container, the whole host goes down, not just the container. 1,2

affected.title: Packets spread across several CPUs
affected.body: Kim says the race needs packets handled concurrently on different CPUs. That's possible when the interface the attacker's traffic arrives on has two or more receive queues, or when RPS (receive packet steering) is turned on for it. The command is a first check: it prints one line per receive queue with its RPS setting. One rx- line for that interface, a setting of all zeros (RPS's default) and RFS (receive flow steering) left off, its default, means you don't meet this condition; RFS is off when /proc/sys/net/core/rps_sock_flow_entries is 0. More lines, or a non-zero setting, means packets can be spread out; whether they actually land on different CPUs depends on which CPUs each queue's interrupt and the RPS setting point to. 1,2,9 grep . /sys/class/net/*/queues/rx-*/rps_cpus

actions.title: Update the kernel and reboot
actions.body: Fixed in the current releases: Debian 12 6.1.192-1, Debian 13 6.12.117-1, RHEL 8 4.18.0-553.189.1.el8_10, RHEL 9.9 5.14.0-741.26.1.el9_9 and RHEL 10.3 6.12.0-264.19.1.el10_3. Red Hat also fixed older update streams: RHEL 8.8 for Telecommunications Update Service and SAP customers in 4.18.0-477.181.1.el8_8 (24 Nov 2026), and RHEL 8.6 (AUS and EUS Long-Life) in 4.18.0-372.230.1.el8_6 and RHEL 10.0 EUS in 6.12.0-55.121.1.el10_0 (27 Nov 2026); it lists no fix yet for other older update streams, such as 9.8 and 10.2. Ubuntu lists fixes in progress for its main kernel on every release from 16.04 to 26.10; most of its other kernels (cloud, HWE, Raspberry Pi and others) are still listed as vulnerable on the releases they ship for, with no fix in progress yet. On Arm and POWER, a netdev review bot asked for this fix to be backported together with the Linux 9.8 race fix, because without it the crash might still be reachable there; no maintainer has confirmed that, and older stable kernels (5.10 to 6.6) have only this fix so far. 3,4,5,6,12,13,14,15 Latest safe versions checked 28 Nov Linux kernel → Debian 13 6.12.118-1 Debian 12 6.1.192-3 Ubuntu 26.04 7.0.0-44.44 Ubuntu 24.04 6.8.0-151.151 Ubuntu 22.04 5.15.0-204.214 RHEL 10.3 6.12.0-264.21.1.el10_3 RHEL 10.2 6.12.0-211.78.1.el10_2 RHEL 9 5.14.0-741.28.1.el9_9 RHEL 8 4.18.0-553.190.1.el8_10 Ubuntu 26.10: 7.3.0-11.12. actions.title: Can't update yet? Two stopgaps
actions.body: Both come from Kim and Red Hat. Turn SYN cookies off by setting net.ipv4.tcp_syncookies to 0; it blocks the SYN cookie path the crash uses, has to be set in each network namespace (so in each container too), and weakens protection against SYN floods. Or cut the receive queues of the internet-facing interface to one and turn RPS and RFS off. 1,2,4

actions.title: Why it isn't Patch now
actions.body: The easy path only crashes servers: Red Hat says it "does not allow data alteration or arbitrary code execution", and the kernel CVE team scores no data impact. Kim calls it remote corruption and describes a second, much harder path that can reach freed memory, which kernel maintainer Eric Dumazet disputed when the fix was first posted. On code execution Kim says "Not yet. and basically, no": he has only "a very limited, lab-specific exploit that targets VM servers", and his GitHub page has no exploit code. No attacks are reported and it isn't on CISA's list of exploited bugs. Ratings differ: the kernel CVE team gives 7.5, Ubuntu High, Red Hat Important (its 7.5 vector assumes an attacker with some privileges who can read and change data, which its own statement rules out), and CISA's entry in the CVE record 5.9, rating the timing hard. We'd change the verdict to Patch now if working exploit code is published or attacks are reported. 1,2,3,4,5,8,11

affected.title: A kernel with the bug, unfixed
affected.body: Xint dates the bug to 4.15 (Jan 2018). The fix names the change that caused it, and that change was also copied into older stable kernels in early 2018: 4.14.16, 4.9.79, 4.4.114, 4.1.50, 3.18.93, 3.16.55 and 3.2.100. So an older version number doesn't rule you out. The fix was merged into the main kernel tree on 19 Nov and first came out in 7.4-rc4 (22 Nov), a test release. The newest stable kernels (7.3.6, 6.18.65, 6.12.119, released 23 Nov) don't have it, and on 28 Nov it wasn't in any of the stable queues (7.3, 6.18, 6.12, 6.6, 6.1, 5.15, 5.10); the only distro kernels we found carrying it are Gentoo's kernel sources and Fedora Rawhide's 7.4-rc4 snapshot builds (Rawhide is Fedora's development branch, not a release). affected.title: Untrusted code can run on it
affected.body: The attacker must already run code on the machine, as any user or inside a container. Xint got there through nginx2root. The bug needs no special rights. Containers don't stop it: they share the host kernel, Docker's default seccomp profile doesn't block SCTP sockets, and Kubernetes pods run without seccomp unless you turn it on. 1,2,9,12,13,14

affected.title: SCTP can load
affected.body: The kernel loads the sctp module the first time any program opens an SCTP socket, unless it's blocked. Many distros ship it. Red Hat says it isn't loaded by default on RHEL: it's in kernel-modules-extra, which blacklists it on install. If lsmod prints nothing, it can still load on demand; modprobe -c | grep sctp shows any block. 1,9,10,11,15 lsmod | grep sctp

actions.title: Block SCTP if you don't use it
actions.body: Put this line in a file under /etc/modprobe.d/ (Ubuntu uses disable-sctp.conf); on Debian and Ubuntu, then run sudo update-initramfs -u . It doesn't unload a module that's already loaded (reboot, or sudo rmmod sctp if nothing uses it) and doesn't help if SCTP is built into the kernel. It breaks telecom signalling and some Kubernetes network plugins. Red Hat's version is install sctp /bin/true plus blacklist sctp . 1,9,10,16 install sctp /bin/false

actions.title: Update the kernel and reboot
actions.body: Install your distro's kernel with the fix ("sctp: do not free a new asoc peeled off while sendmsg slept") once it ships, then reboot. The 23 Nov stable releases (7.3.6, 6.18.65, 6.12.119) don't have it, and on 28 Nov it wasn't in any of the stable queues (7.3, 6.18, 6.12, 6.6, 6.1, 5.15, 5.10); Debian unstable's 7.3.6-1 doesn't have it either. No release date is announced and the fix has no CVE yet; we'll check again by 2 Dec 2026. 2,3,4,18,19,21,23,24,25

actions.title: Patch the way in
actions.body: Xint's chain starts with nginx2root, so upgrade nginx too. Any other way to run code on the host or in a container works just as well. 1,7

affected.body: GET /login needs no login. The page decrypted the login_error cookie before it tried OAuth auto-login, and the decryption doesn't need OAuth to be set up. 10,2

affected.title: They already have Grafana's encrypted data
affected.body: The bug only turns ciphertext the instance produced back into plaintext: for example data source passwords and contact point credentials. On its own it reveals nothing, so it matters where a database copy, backup or leaked row is in someone else's hands. 2,9

actions.title: Update Grafana
actions.body: Update to 13.3.2, 13.2.7, 13.1.11, 13.0.14 or 12.4.16 (24 Nov 2026), which fix all three bugs. Older lines, such as 12.3, get no more patches: upgrade to a supported line.

actions.title: Our precaution: rotate secrets
actions.body: Grafana hasn't said to rotate anything; this is our advice. If a copy of Grafana's database or a backup has ever left your control, we'd rotate the data source and contact point credentials stored in Grafana, because the login bug could have turned them into plaintext. If Editors you don't fully trust could test contact points, we'd rotate contact point credentials too, because the contact point bug could have sent them to their own URL. 1,2

actions.title: The other two fixes
actions.body: These matter if someone you don't fully trust has Editor access. Contact point tests: an Editor could test an existing contact point under a different schema version or type, point it at their own URL and have its stored secrets sent there; secrets echoed in notifier errors also came back to the caller. Snapshots (12.4 to 13.2): the newer snapshot API checked only the delete permission Editors have, not "creator or can edit the dashboard" like the old API. The 24 Nov releases add that check; 13.3 fixed it in 13.3.0. 2,3,11,4,7,8

actions.title: Which CVE is which
actions.body: Grafana hasn't published advisories or CVE records yet. Our reading of the code: the snapshot fix matches CVE-2026-88943, the one ID missing from 13.3.2's notes; the login and contact point fixes are CVE-2026-107561 and CVE-2026-88960, in an order Grafana hasn't said. We'll check again for Grafana's advisory by 2 Dec 2026. 1,2

actions.title: Why it isn't Patch now
actions.body: No exploit or attacks are known, it isn't on CISA's exploited list, the login bug needs data the attacker would already have to have stolen, and the other two need an Editor login. We'd raise it if an exploit appears or attacks are reported. 1,2,6

affected.title: pam-mysql checks your logins
affected.body: The module is in the PAM setup of a login service such as sshd, the case the researcher tested. Every released version has the bug, 0.8.x and the 1.0.0 betas. Few systems use it: Debian counts 190 installs. A file name in the output means it's in use for that service. 1,10 grep -rl pam_mysql /etc/pam.d/

affected.title: The service refuses empty passwords
affected.body: That is sshd's default ( PermitEmptyPasswords no ), and it's what triggers the bug: sshd asks pam-mysql to refuse accounts with no password, and pam-mysql does the opposite. Don't switch it to yes as a fix; the researcher says that opens a different hole. Run as root. 1,5 sshd -T | grep -i permitemptypasswords

affected.title: Some accounts have no password
affected.body: At least one row in the login table has no stored password. On 0.8.x (Debian, Ubuntu, Gentoo, FreeBSD) that means NULL. On the 1.0.0 betas (Fedora, Nix, Mageia, ALT) an empty string counts too, so the common NOT NULL DEFAULT '' column is exposed; the researcher says PostfixAdmin and Froxlor ship tables like that. Replace the table and column names with yours. 1 SELECT username FROM users WHERE password IS NULL OR password='';
code: SELECT username FROM users WHERE password IS NULL OR password='';

affected.body: Fixed: Debian 13 0.8.2-2.1+deb13u1 and Debian 12 0.8.2-2+deb12u1 . Some news sites give 0.8.2-2.1 as fixed for Debian 13; Debian lists that version as vulnerable. actions.title: Update the package

actions.title: No update yet? Fill the gaps
actions.body: Stop storing accounts with no password in any table used for logins: delete those rows, then make the password column NOT NULL with no empty-string default. That's the researcher's fix for unpatched systems. Don't set PermitEmptyPasswords yes . 1

actions.title: Check past logins
actions.body: sshd logs a bypass exactly like a normal login ("Accepted password for"). Any password login by an account that had no stored password at the time was a bypass. The table as it is now may not show what it held then; a backup or the binary log does. pam-mysql's own log table is off by default, and when on it spells failures AUTHENTICATION FALURE . 1

affected.title: Rules use EndpointRequest or the H2 console matcher
affected.body: Your Spring Security config builds rules with EndpointRequest (Actuator, servlet or reactive) or PathRequest.toH2Console() . The fix didn't change the static-resource matchers. 1,2

affected.body: For example management.endpoints.web.path-mapping.health=status/ or spring.h2.console.path=/custom/ , which produce a rule for /actuator/status//** that never matches /actuator/status . affected.title: A later rule is looser

affected.title: WhatsApp older than its fix
affected.body: The IP address bug (CVE-2026-23871) is in WhatsApp and WhatsApp Business for Android from 2.20.198.3, before 2.26.17.4. The order-message bug (CVE-2026-102769) is in WhatsApp for Android before 2.26.35.74; its description names only WhatsApp for Android, but the same record also lists WhatsApp Business for Android from 2.22.3.7, before 2.26.35.74. affected.title: An attacker in the right position
affected.body: For the IP address bug, that's anyone who can send you a crafted Click to WhatsApp ad-reply message: once it's shown in a chat, your phone can fetch media from the attacker's server and reveal your IP address. For the order-message bug, you have to tap a crafted "order details" message sent from an unofficial WhatsApp client; it can delete WhatsApp's own locally stored files, and leak one bit of information about your chat database if you're online when it arrives. For the Meta AI bug, the attacker has to be inside Meta's infrastructure, and Meta says a third-party transparency ledger confirms no exploitation. 2,3,4

affected.body: Every earlier 11.0, 10.1 and 9.0 release; end-of-life 8.5 and older get no fixes. The critical cluster bug is the exception: it affects only 11.0.29, 10.1.62 and 9.0.124. Spring Boot embeds Tomcat, and its newest releases (4.2.0, 4.1.3 and 4.0.10) still bring in 11.0.27; check with ./mvnw dependency:tree -Dincludes=org.apache.tomcat.embed . 1,2,3,13,14 $CATALINA_HOME/bin/version.sh

affected.title: You turned on an affected feature
affected.body: Ten of the 11 need something you add: HTTP/2 (an Http2Protocol line inside a <Connector> ; in Spring Boot, server.http2.enabled ), the RewriteValve, the ExpiresFilter, CGI, Jakarta Authentication, clustering, an AJP load balancer or the OWB module. The shipped files contain commented-out examples, so matches inside <!-- --> don't count. Check your apps' WEB-INF/web.xml and META-INF/context.xml too. The eleventh, a low-rated memory leak (CVE-2026-118233), needs an app that uses the HTTP upgrade API; Apache only says "some circumstances". 1,10,11,16,17 grep -rnE 'Http2Protocol|RewriteValve|ExpiresFilter|CGIServlet|<Cluster|LoadBalancerDrainingValve|OpenWebBeans' $CATALINA_BASE/conf/

actions.title: Upgrade to 11.0.29, 10.1.62 or 9.0.124
actions.body: Released 13 to 16 Nov 2026, these fix 9 of the 11 bugs; the two cluster bugs aren't fixed in them (see below). actions.title: Clusters: stay on TLS 1.2
actions.body: If your cluster uses TLS-PSK, keep it on TLS 1.2: on TLS 1.3 a node without the key can join (CVE-2026-133325). detail.verdictHint: Scored 9.8; Red Hat: weak-order CPUs only, crash only.
detail.meterHint: Patch on schedule. Watch for news.

affected.title: Kernel 5.4.208 or later, unpatched
affected.body: The race came in with a refcount change in 5.5 (also backported to 5.4 from 5.4.208). Upstream fixes: 6.12.118, 6.18.64, 7.3.5 and 7.4-rc2; the CVE record lists no fix yet for the 6.6, 6.1, 5.15, 5.10 and 5.4 lines. Red Hat says RHEL 7 and 8 are not affected. Distro kernels backport, so compare with your distro's version under Update. 1,4 uname -r

affected.title: A weakly ordered processor
affected.body: The CVE record says the change behind the bug removed the ordering on weakly ordered architectures, and Red Hat says triggering it needs weakly ordered hardware. Arm says 64-bit Arm (Armv8-A) is weakly ordered, and POWER is too; x86 has the strongest ordering of the common architectures. uname -m shows the architecture, for example aarch64 (Arm) or ppc64le (POWER). 1,4,7,9 uname -m

affected.title: An attacker who can reach a TCP port
affected.body: The kernel CVE team's scoring says an attacker produces the race by opening and closing connections and sending more TCP segments while sockets are being reused, with no login. Red Hat calls the timing high-complexity. 1,4

actions.title: Update the kernel as usual
actions.body: Debian 13 has the fix in 6.12.118-1 (DSA-6652-1). Debian 12, Ubuntu 20.04 to 26.10 and Ubuntu 18.04's 5.4 kernels ( linux-hwe-5.4 and the cloud and Raspberry Pi 5.4 kernels) are still listed as vulnerable, and Red Hat has deferred the fix for RHEL 9 and 10, so take it when your distro ships it. Red Hat, Ubuntu and Debian list no workaround. 4,5,6 Latest safe versions checked 28 Nov Linux kernel → Debian 13 6.12.118-1 Debian 12 6.1.192-3 Ubuntu 26.04 7.0.0-44.44 Ubuntu 24.04 6.8.0-151.151 Ubuntu 22.04 5.15.0-204.214 RHEL 10.3 6.12.0-264.21.1.el10_3 RHEL 10.2 6.12.0-211.78.1.el10_2 RHEL 9 5.14.0-741.28.1.el9_9 RHEL 8 4.18.0-553.190.1.el8_10 Ubuntu 26.10: 7.3.0-11.12. Cloud and HWE kernels have their own versions.

actions.title: Why it isn't Patch now
actions.body: The kernel CVE team scored it 9.8, arguing the race can lead to use of freed memory. Red Hat currently rates it 5.9 (Moderate): "restricting the impact strictly to a denial of service", and says it can't be used to run code or expose data. Ubuntu rates it Medium. Hyunwoo Kim, who wrote the fix, asked "Who slapped a 9.8 on this?" No exploit or attacks are known, and it isn't on CISA's list of exploited bugs. We'd change the verdict if anyone shows it working against a real system. 1,2,3,4,5,8

affected.title: OpenSSL 4.0.0 to 4.0.3, or 4.1.0
affected.body: OpenSSL's CVE record lists only these versions; 3.x and older are not listed. Ubuntu disagrees in one place: it marks the Node.js package on Ubuntu 22.04, which bundles OpenSSL 1.1.1m, as vulnerable. Apps can also bundle their own OpenSSL. 1,7 openssl version

affected.title: Something encodes ~1.6 GB at once
affected.body: A program has to pass more than (INT_MAX / 4) * 3 bytes, about 1.6 GB, to EVP_EncodeBlock() in one call. The fix's pull request named the proxy login of openssl s_client -proxy_pass as a path, but OpenSSL's CVE record now says the command-line tools can't practically be made to do it, and that TLS, QUIC and CMS never encode buffers that size. The fix changes only the base64 code and the HTTP proxy login code. 1,2

affected.title: An attacker controls that data
affected.body: OpenSSL says only an app that takes a length from an attacker and passes it to EVP_EncodeBlock() without its own check is exposed, and it knows of no such path. CISA's score, now 5.9 (Medium), still assumes a remote attacker with no login; NVD hasn't scored it itself. 1,5

actions.title: Update when 4.1.1 / 4.0.4 ship
actions.body: OpenSSL's CVE record names 4.1.1 and 4.0.4 as the first fixed versions, and OpenSSL has scheduled those releases for 1 Dec 2026. On 23 Nov the fix was still unmerged, on hold for discussion with changes requested, so check the release notes. 1,4,2,9,7,8

actions.title: Only use proxy passwords you set
actions.body: If you script openssl s_client -proxy_pass , don't let other people supply the password or the environment variable it's read from. 2

actions.title: Cap input in your own code
actions.body: If your code calls EVP_EncodeBlock() on data from others, reject inputs over (INT_MAX / 4) * 3 bytes. That's the limit OpenSSL's fix enforces. 2
